nameStory: Desmodesmus opoliensis doesn't have a widely-used common name since it's a microscopic green algae that most people never notice. The scientific name comes from 'desmos' meaning chain or bond, and 'scenos' meaning scene or stage, referring to how these tiny cells link together in small groups. The species name 'opoliensis' likely refers to Opole, a region in Poland where it may have been first described.
description: This is a microscopic single-celled green algae that you'll never see with the naked eye - it's only about 10-20 micrometers across (that's smaller than the width of a human hair!). Under a microscope, it appears as tiny green oval cells that often stick together in groups of 2-4 cells. Like other green algae, it contains chlorophyll and makes its own food through photosynthesis, giving it a bright green color. You'd need a microscope with at least 400x magnification to really see its details.

idTips.label: Cell arrangement
idTips.description: Cells typically form small colonies of 2-4 cells arranged in a single row, looking like tiny green beads strung together under the microscope

idTips.label: Cell shape
idTips.description: Individual cells are oval to elliptical with slightly pointed ends, giving them a football-like appearance when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright grass-green color due to chlorophyll, with the green evenly distributed throughout each cell

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely tiny - individual cells are only 10-20 micrometers long, invisible without significant magnification

idTips.label: Cell wall features
idTips.description: Smooth cell walls without the spines or projections found on some related species

habitat: Found floating freely in freshwater environments including ponds, lakes, slow-moving streams, and temporary pools throughout New England. Prefers nutrient-rich waters and can be common in areas with some organic pollution. Often discovered in water samples collected from suburban ponds or farm runoff areas.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water temperatures warm and daylight increases. Best time to find them in water samples from shallow, warming ponds.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when populations can bloom in nutrient-rich waters. Most likely to be detected in microscopic examination of pond water.
seasonality.fall: Still present but populations may decline as temperatures cool and daylight decreases. Can persist in protected water bodies.
seasonality.winter: Present but dormant in ice-covered waters. Populations are typically at their lowest levels during the coldest months.

funFact: Despite being incredibly tiny, a single drop of pond water can contain thousands of these algae cells, and they're actually helping to produce much of the oxygen we breathe - freshwater algae like this species contribute significantly to global oxygen production!
confusionNotes: Under the microscope, it's easily confused with other small green algae in the Scenedesmaceae family. The key is looking for the specific 2-4 cell colonies arranged in a single row - other species might form different patterns or have spines on their cell walls.
contextualKnowledge: This is a relatively recently described species with very few recorded observations in New England, so finding it would be quite noteworthy for citizen science projects. Most people associate algae with the slimy green stuff in ponds, but microscopic species like this are actually the foundation of freshwater food webs.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives like Desmodesmus communis, this species lacks the prominent spines or teeth on the outer cells that characterize many other Desmodesmus species. Desmodesmus denticulatus has obvious tooth-like projections, while D. opoliensis has smooth, clean cell walls. The cell arrangement pattern and smooth margins are the key distinguishing features from other members of this genus.
